paragraphs.source_en: Growing up in my home was often painful because Dad would make us take responsibility for everything. If I came home from school and said something like, “My girlfriend makes me so mad!” Dad would respond by saying, “No one can make you mad unless you let them, Sean. It’s your choice.” Or if I grumbled, “I can’t stand my math teacher. I’m going to flunk algebra because of him!” Dad would take me aside and gently say, “Sean, listen to your language. If you flunk algebra, it’s your fault, not your teacher’s. And instead of *talking about* your teacher, why not *talk with* him about how to improve things in class?” I’d think, “Are you serious, Dad? You don’t get it.” And then I’d go find Mom, who let me blame other people for my problems. It was a good balance: Dad was always loyal to principles, while Mom was always loyal to you.

paragraphs.source_en: Many years ago, my dad asked me how work was going. I began listing my complaints: “It’s hard to juggle so much.” “The office politics are terrible.” “I’m totally burned out.” “My long commute is killing me.” And on and on. I was hoping for a little sympathy. Instead, Dad looked at me disappointedly and said, “Geez, Sean. That doesn’t sound like you. Why are you being such a victim? Organize your time so that you’re not so busy. Don’t get your head into office politics. If you don’t like your long commute, then move.” He then walked away. I was taken aback but suddenly realized, “He’s absolutely right. I *am* being a victim. How did this happen? Stop it right now!” It was a good wakeup call. Yes, I was free to choose my attitude, my level of busyness, my commute, and my response to everything that was happening to me! I felt so grateful for the reminder.
